text:
Based strictly on the provided text, education in New Zealand is a free, compulsory, and secular national state system established on January 1, 1878, following the abolition of provincial governments. Compulsory attendance is mandatory between the ages of 6 and 16, though most students start primary school around age 5 and continue until at least age 17. The system is structured into 13 year levels: primary education spans years 1 through 8 (with years 7 and 8 known as intermediate), and secondary education covers years 9 through 13. Students generally transition to secondary education at ages 12 to 13. All state and state-integrated schools follow the national curriculum, *The New Zealand Curriculum* (for English-medium schools) or *Te Marautanga o Aotearoa* (for Māori-medium schools), while private schools must have an equivalent curriculum.
The system consists of three funding types: state schools (government-owned and free), state-integrated schools (government-funded but charge compulsory attendance dues to maintain special character, often religious), and private schools (funded primarily by tuition fees). Early childhood education includes center-based services like kindergartens and parent-led options like *Kohanga Reo* (language nests). A significant focus exists on Māori education, with efforts to revive the language through immersion schools ( *Kura Kaupapa Māori* ) and bicultural programs, recognizing Māori as an official language. Tertiary education is regulated by the New Zealand Qualifications Framework and funded through a combination of government subsidies and student loans/allowances, with recent concerns noted regarding high fees and skills shortages. While the system is highly regarded, challenges such as school bullying and the need to improve academic achievement for Māori and Pacific Island students have been identified.
